reference.source: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children, and Adolescents
clinicalPearls: Parachute mitral valve has all chordae inserting into a single dominant papillary muscle, producing subvalvar inflow obstruction and congenital mitral stenosis.
It is the classic component of Shone complex alongside supravalvar mitral ring, subaortic stenosis and coarctation, so the other three lesions should always be sought.
Obstruction occurs at the interchordal level, so the mitral orifice can look adequate while flow is restricted between crowded chordae.
Parasternal short-axis imaging shows a single papillary muscle with limited leaflet opening and a narrow subvalvar funnel.
A true parachute with one papillary muscle is distinguished from a parachute-like asymmetric valve, which has two papillary muscles, one of them hypoplastic.
Symptoms track the gradient and include dyspnoea, poor feeding and pulmonary hypertension in infants.
Surgery is technically difficult; splitting the papillary muscle or fenestrating chordae may relieve obstruction, but replacement is sometimes required.
reference.pathophysiology: In a true parachute mitral valve all chordae tendineae converge and insert into a single papillary muscle, while in the parachute-like asymmetric variant they insert into one dominant papillary muscle with a hypoplastic second muscle. The interchordal spaces are markedly reduced, so blood entering the left ventricle must pass through the crowded, narrowed spaces between chordae, generating functional stenosis at the subvalvar level even when the annular orifice appears normal. The lesion frequently coexists with other left-heart obstructive anomalies as part of Shone complex, compounding the inflow and outflow obstruction.
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic echocardiography with short-axis papillary muscle count and Doppler inflow gradients
Aortic arch imaging to screen for Shone-complex lesions
Electrocardiography for right ventricular hypertrophy and left atrial enlargement
redFlags: Heart failure or failure to thrive in infancy
Severe inflow gradient with low cardiac output
reference.prognosis: Isolated mild parachute valve may be well tolerated, but significant stenosis, especially within Shone complex, carries higher surgical risk and a tendency to residual or recurrent obstruction requiring reintervention.
pitfalls: Overlooking subvalvar obstruction when the annulus and orifice appear normal
Failing to identify associated Shone-complex lesions
Confusing the lesion with supravalvar mitral ring or cor triatriatum
Assuming a successful repair is durable when restenosis is common
references: Moss and Adams' Heart Disease in Infants, Children, and Adolescents
Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
management: Surgical relief of significant subvalvar mitral stenosis by valve repair, splitting fused chordae and the papillary muscle, or mitral valve replacement when repair is not feasible
Concurrent correction of associated Shone-complex lesions such as supravalvar mitral ring resection, subaortic stenosis relief and coarctation repair
Medical management of pulmonary congestion and heart failure with diuretics while optimising for surgery
Treatment of secondary pulmonary hypertension and monitoring of its progression
Serial echocardiographic surveillance of the inflow gradient, ventricular function and pulmonary pressures, with reintervention for residual or recurrent obstruction
Management within a paediatric and congenital cardiology and cardiac-surgery multidisciplinary team
